name: Lawrence Summers
summary: World Bank chief economist 1991-1993. A memo dated 12 December 1991, signed by him, said the economic logic of dumping toxic waste in the lowest-wage country was 'impeccable'; The Economist published part of it on 8 February 1992. Economist Lant Pritchett says he wrote it as an ironic aside. Summers was later US Treasury Secretary (1999-2001), was paid by hedge fund D. E. Shaw and by Wall Street firms for speeches, and consulted for Citigroup until 2013.

posts.role: Vice President, Development Economics, and Chief Economist
Under Secretary for International Affairs, then Deputy Secretary

name: Joseph Stiglitz
summary: World Bank senior vice president and chief economist 1997-2000. He publicly criticised IMF policies during the Asian crisis. His resignation was announced in November 1999; Robert Wade (New Left Review) and The Nation reported that Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers made Wolfensohn's second term conditional on Stiglitz leaving. His book Globalization and Its Discontents (2002) set out his critique.

posts.role: Senior Vice President and Chief Economist

name: Jim Yong Kim
summary: World Bank president 2012-2019. On 7 January 2019 the Bank announced he would step down on 1 February 2019, more than three years before his term ended; he joined the private infrastructure investor Global Infrastructure Partners as vice chairman and partner.

name: David Malpass
summary: Bear Stearns chief economist in the years before its 2008 collapse, founder of research firm Encima Global in 2008, US Treasury under secretary for international affairs from 2017, then World Bank president from 9 April 2019 to 1 June 2023.

name: Ajay Banga
summary: Mastercard president and CEO, then vice chairman of private-equity firm General Atlantic, before becoming World Bank president on 2 June 2023 after nomination by the Biden administration.

posts.role: President and CEO, then Executive Chairman

name: Kristalina Georgieva
summary: World Bank CEO from January 2017 (interim president February-April 2019) and IMF managing director since October 2019, reappointed in 2024. On the Congo roads case she said the Bank accepted 'full responsibility to correct weaknesses'. A 2021 WilmerHale inquiry for the World Bank alleged that she and other senior officials put 'undue pressure' on staff to change data that raised China's ranking in Doing Business 2018; she denied it, and the IMF board said the evidence did not conclusively show an improper role.

posts.role: Commissioner for International Cooperation, Humanitarian Aid and Crisis Response; then Vice-President for Budget and Human Resources

name: A. W. (Tom) Clausen
summary: President and CEO of Bank of America from 1970, World Bank president July 1981 to June 1986, then back at Bank of America as chairman and CEO until May 1990. The Bank approved its Polonoroeste loans in 1981-82 and a second Chixoy loan of $44.6 million in 1985 during his presidency.

name: Barber Conable
summary: US congressman 1965-1985, then World Bank president 1986-1991. In 1987 he called Polonoroeste, the road and settlement programme in Brazil's Amazon that the Bank had funded with about $445-500 million, a 'sobering example' of an environmentally sound effort gone wrong.

name: Lewis Preston
summary: Joined J.P. Morgan in 1951 and was its chairman and CEO from 1980 to 1989 and chairman of its executive committee until 1991, then World Bank president from 1 September 1991 until his death on 4 May 1995.

posts.role: Chairman and CEO; then chairman of the executive committee

name: Eugene R. Black
summary: Vice president, later senior vice president, of Chase National Bank from 1933, US executive director at the World Bank from 1947, then World Bank president from 1 July 1949 to 31 December 1962. During his presidency the Bank lent $80 million in 1956 for the Kariba dam, $35 million in 1959 for the COMILOG manganese mine in Gabon, and $47 million in 1962 for Ghana's Akosombo dam.

posts.role: Vice President, then Senior Vice President

name: Mohamed El-Erian
summary: Fifteen years at the IMF, rising to deputy director, then managing director at Salomon Smith Barney/Citigroup in London, then PIMCO from 1999. He ran Harvard's endowment for about two years, rejoined PIMCO at the end of 2007 and became its CEO and co-chief investment officer until 2014. He later became chief economic adviser at Allianz, PIMCO's parent.

name: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
summary: Spent 25 years at the World Bank, rising to managing director 2007-2011, around two terms as Nigeria's finance minister (2003-2006 and 2011-2015). After the fuel subsidy was removed in January 2012 and petrol more than doubled, she publicly defended it as 'subsidy reallocation' with 'clear and measurable benefits'; police shot protesters. She joined Twitter's board in 2018 and became WTO director-general in 2021.

posts.role: Coordinating Minister for the Economy and Minister of Finance

name: Kemal Derviş
summary: World Bank staffer from 1977, vice president for the Middle East and North Africa (1996) and for poverty reduction and economic management (2000). On 13 March 2001 he became Turkey's minister for economic affairs and led its IMF-backed recovery programme. Turkey's June 2001 letter of intent to the IMF made a new Tobacco Law a loan condition and committed to privatise the tobacco factories, which ended in Tekel's sale to British American Tobacco in 2008. He later headed UNDP.

posts.role: Staff; Vice President, Middle East and North Africa (1996); Vice President, Poverty Reduction and Economic Management (2000)
Minister of State for Economic Affairs and the Treasury
Vice President, Global Economy and Development

name: Domingo Cavallo
summary: Central bank president in 1982, economy minister 1991-1996 and again in 2001 under IMF-supported financing. On 1 December 2001 he announced a $250-a-week cap on cash withdrawals (the corralito) and resigned during the 19-20 December protests in which 39 people were killed. He was sentenced in 2015 to three and a half years in the salary-bonus case; Argentina's Supreme Court threw out the case in November 2024 because it had run 18 years.

name: Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada
summary: Mining businessman (COMSUR) who, as Senate president, coordinated the 1985 task force that drafted Bolivia's Decree 21060, then planning minister and president of Bolivia 1993-1997 and 2002-2003. In February 2003 his government announced an income tax to meet a deficit target in IMF talks; a police strike and deadly clashes followed and it was withdrawn. After the October 2003 killings he left for the US, where a federal jury in 2018 found him liable for extrajudicial killings and awarded $10 million; the verdict was reinstated in 2021.

name: Carlos Andrés Pérez
summary: President of Venezuela 1974-1979 and 1989-1993. On 16 February 1989 he announced adjustment measures agreed with the IMF; gasoline price rises set off the Caracazo, and he called out the army. Officials first gave 276 dead; the Inter-American Court later ruled against Venezuela. Impeached in 1993 over a 250-million-bolívar secret fund, he was convicted in May 1996 of misuse of public funds, acquitted of embezzlement, and given 28 months of house arrest.

name: Hugo Banzer
summary: Military ruler of Bolivia 1971-1978 and elected president 1997-2001. Under his government Cochabamba's water went to the Bechtel-led Aguas del Tunari, after World Bank advice that tariff rises should not be softened by subsidies. When protests grew he declared a state of siege on 8 April 2000; the US State Department reported four civilians killed in April, at least three by security forces.

name: Jeffrey Sachs
summary: Harvard economist who advised Bolivia's 1985 stabilisation (Decree 21060: wage freeze, subsidy cuts, a floated currency), followed by an IMF standby in June 1986 and mass tin-mine closures. He then advised Poland (1989) and Russia on rapid transition, working with David Lipton. He co-wrote the NBER account of Bolivia's programme.

name: Suharto
summary: President of Indonesia 1967-1998. In 1995 he ordered Jakarta's water service split between Thames Water (with his son as partner) and Suez (with the Salim Group). On 15 January 1998 he signed a new IMF agreement; fuel prices rose under the programme in May 1998, followed by riots, and he resigned on 21 May 1998. Transparency International in 2004 put alleged embezzlement during his rule at $15-35 billion.

name: Frederick Chiluba
summary: President of Zambia 1991-2002. His government sold the state copper company ZCCM, completed in 2000, including Konkola to Anglo American and Mufulira to Glencore-led Mopani. On 4 May 2007 London's High Court found in a civil case that he and associates stole $46 million; in August 2009 a Zambian court acquitted him of criminal charges of embezzling $500,000.

name: Lenín Moreno
summary: Vice president of Ecuador 2007-2013 and president 2017-2021. He took a $4.2 billion IMF loan in March 2019 within a financing package of more than $10 billion; his Decree 883 ended fuel subsidies in October 2019, protests followed, the Ombudsman counted 11 dead, and he withdrew the decree. On 28 August 2026 Ecuador's National Court sentenced him to five years for bribery over the Coca Codo Sinclair dam built by Sinohydro.

name: William Ruto
summary: President of Kenya since 2022. He signed the Finance Act 2023 into law on 26 June 2023 during an IMF programme. The Finance Bill 2024 set off protests in which 60 people died, per Kenya's national rights commission as cited by Amnesty; on 26 June 2024 he declined to sign it and it was withdrawn, and he later dismissed most of his cabinet.

name: Selby Wilson
summary: Trinidad and Tobago finance minister during the 1988-1989 IMF stand-by. He told the official Commission of Enquiry into the 1990 coup attempt that to meet IMF targets 'it was either we sent home 15,000 people or cut salaries'; public pay was cut 10%. The Commission named the IMF programme and the pay cut among policies that 'greatly upset and angered' the public.

name: Enrique Mathov
summary: Argentina's security secretary in December 2001. In May 2016 Federal Oral Court No. 6 convicted him of negligent homicide over police killings during the 20 December 2001 protests in Buenos Aires and sentenced him to four years and nine months; police chief Rubén Santos got four years.

name: Masupha Sole
summary: Chief executive of the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority on the World Bank-backed Lesotho Highlands Water Project. Lesotho's High Court convicted him in 2002 of taking bribes from international contractors and consultants through intermediaries and sentenced him to 18 years; the Court of Appeal cut this to 15 years in April 2003. Firms that bribed him, Acres International and Lahmeyer International, were convicted in Lesotho and later barred by the World Bank (Acres 2004, Lahmeyer 2006).

name: Roberto David Castillo
summary: President of DESA, the company building the Agua Zarca dam, owned by Castillo and the Atala Zablah family, and a US-trained former Honduran army intelligence officer. Berta Cáceres, who led opposition to the dam, was murdered on 2 March 2016. On 5 July 2021 a Honduran court found Castillo a co-perpetrator in planning the killing; in June 2022 he was sentenced to 22 years and six months, and in November 2024 the Supreme Court rejected his appeal.

name: Cyril Ramaphosa
summary: Former mineworkers' union leader who was a non-executive director of Lonmin, an IFC client, in 2012. The day before police killed 34 strikers at Marikana, he emailed Lonmin that the events were 'plainly dastardly criminal' and that there needed to be 'concomitant action'. The Farlam Commission (2015) absolved him of wrongdoing. He apologised for the emails' wording in 2017 and became South Africa's president in 2018.

name: Paul Singer
summary: Founder of hedge fund Elliott Management and its offshore unit NML Capital, which buy defaulted government debt cheaply and sue for full payment. Elliott paid about $11 million in 1996 for $20 million of Peruvian debt and collected $58 million in 2000 after suing. In 2012 NML obtained a Ghanaian court order detaining the Argentine navy ship ARA Libertad; the Law of the Sea tribunal ordered its release.

name: John Perkins
summary: Peace Corps volunteer in Ecuador 1968-1970, then chief economist at the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main in the 1970s, where he says he advised the World Bank, IMF and UN. His 2004 book Confessions of an Economic Hit Man claims the NSA arranged his hiring and that his job was to inflate forecasts so countries took on unpayable debt. These are his claims, not confirmed by documents.

name: Fábio Schvartsman
summary: Vale chief executive from May 2017 until he took leave in March 2019. Charged with qualified homicide and environmental crimes over the 25 January 2019 Córrego do Feijão dam collapse, reported as killing 270 people (272 in one report). A regional court halted the case; Brazil's Superior Court of Justice put him back as a defendant in April 2026 and refused his appeal in June 2026. He has not been tried.

name: Ricardo Vescovi de Aragão
summary: Samarco president when the Fundão dam failed in 2015, killing 19 people. Prosecuted in the criminal case and acquitted in November 2024. A federal appeal court kept his acquittal in September 2026, while convicting Samarco and three former managers.

posts.years: at the time of the 2015 collapse

name: Beny Steinmetz
summary: Diamond and mining investor behind Beny Steinmetz Group Resources (BSGR), the group that Koidu Holdings belonged to when police shot two people dead at a 2007 protest at the Koidu mine in Sierra Leone. OCCRP reports he flew to Freetown in May 2008 and met the president, after which the government let the halted mine restart. He is not accused over the shootings.

posts.role: Namesake of the group; described his role as "ambassadorial"

name: Sergio Ramón Rodríguez Orellana
summary: DESA's communities and environment manager on the Agua Zarca dam. Convicted over the 2016 murder of Berta Cáceres and sentenced to 30 years. In February 2025 the full Supreme Court upheld the sentence and changed his role from co-author to instigator.

posts.years: at the time of the 2016 murder

name: Douglas Geovanny Bustillo
summary: Former head of DESA's private security on the Agua Zarca dam, and a former army lieutenant. He left DESA in July 2015 and kept in contact with its president. Convicted over the 2016 murder of Berta Cáceres and sentenced to 30 years; the Supreme Court's Criminal Chamber upheld the conviction in November 2024.

name: Daniel Atala Midence
summary: DESA's chief financial officer. Honduran prosecutors charged him in December 2023 as a suspected mastermind of the 2016 murder of Berta Cáceres, and a court issued an arrest warrant. He has not been arrested or tried on any page opened; a 2026 report calls him a fugitive. His lawyer has said he denies any part in the crime.

posts.years: at the time of the 2016 murder

name: Pedro Atala Zablah
summary: DESA board member. In an October 2015 company chat he wrote "It's them or us" about COPINH, the group led by Berta Cáceres, according to phone data reported by The Intercept. COPINH names him among those responsible for her 2016 murder. He has not been charged on any page opened, and his lawyer denies any part in the crime.

posts.years: at the time of the 2016 murder

name: Ian Lundin
summary: Chief executive, Lundin Oil (now Orrön Energy). On trial in Stockholm since September 2023, charged with complicity in war crimes in Sudan. Prosecutors say the two men asked the government to make its army responsible for security at a Lundin exploration site, which led to bombing, killing of civilians and burned villages from 1999 to 2003. Verdict due 17 February 2027.

name: Alex Schneiter
summary: Vice president, Lundin Oil (now Orrön Energy). On trial in Stockholm since September 2023, charged with complicity in war crimes in Sudan. Prosecutors say the two men asked the government to make its army responsible for security at a Lundin exploration site, which led to bombing, killing of civilians and burned villages from 1999 to 2003. Verdict due 17 February 2027.

posts.years: at the time of the alleged conduct

name: Iskandar Safa
summary: Owner and chief executive of Privinvest, the shipbuilder paid under Mozambique's hidden loans. He died in January 2024. London's High Court found in July 2024 that he was "the individual ultimately behind each promise and payment" to finance minister Manuel Chang. This is a civil finding. The Court of Appeal struck out the Privinvest companies' appeal in May 2026 for failing to meet its terms.

name: Jean Boustani
summary: Privinvest salesman and negotiator tried in New York over kickbacks tied to Mozambique's hidden loans. A US jury acquitted him of all three conspiracy counts in December 2019.

name: Andrew Pearse
summary: Former senior Credit Suisse banker who helped arrange the Mozambique loans. Pleaded guilty in the US in July 2019 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and testified against Jean Boustani. Sentenced to time served in March 2025, with payments and forfeitures. The UK financial regulator banned him the same month.

posts.years: at the time of the loans

name: Albert Jamieson
summary: Lonmin chief commercial officer during the 2012 Marikana strike. He told the Farlam Commission he wanted Cyril Ramaphosa to press politicians, and agreed "It's not the right use of political pressure". A legal team at the commission said he and others should be investigated. No charge is reported on the pages opened.

name: Barnard Mokwena
summary: Lonmin's senior human resources executive and a main company voice in the August 2012 strike. He met union leaders and police generals the day before the shooting and told the Farlam Commission that Lonmin would have negotiated only through the NUM union. He retracted claims he had made against the rival union. A legal team at the commission said he should be investigated. No charge is reported on the pages opened.

posts.role: Vice-president, human resources (Miningmx); executive president of human capital and external affairs (IOL, Jacaranda)

name: Keshub Mahindra
summary: Non-executive chairman of Union Carbide India Ltd at the 1984 Bhopal gas leak. A Bhopal court convicted him in June 2010 of causing death by negligence: two years in prison and a Rs 1 lakh fine. He was bailed right after sentencing and appealed. He died in April 2023, aged 99; appeals in the case were still pending in January 2026.

posts.years: at the time of the 1984 leak

name: Vijay Gokhale
summary: Managing director of Union Carbide India Ltd at the 1984 Bhopal gas leak. A Bhopal court convicted him in June 2010 of causing death by negligence: two years in prison and a Rs 1 lakh fine. He was bailed right after sentencing and appealed; appeals were still pending in January 2026. One source spells the name Gokhle.

posts.years: at the time of the 1984 leak

name: Warren Anderson
summary: Chairman and chief executive of Union Carbide at the 1984 Bhopal gas leak. Arrested in India on 4 December 1984 and bailed. A Bhopal magistrate declared him absconding in 1992 for not appearing. He was never tried. He died on 29 September 2014.

posts.years: at the time of the 1984 leak

name: Claude Dauphin
summary: Trafigura founder and director. Jailed in Abidjan in September 2006, weeks after the Probo Koala's waste was dumped, on accusations of breaking toxic waste law and poisoning. Freed in February 2007 after Trafigura paid Côte d'Ivoire about $200 million without admitting liability. Dutch prosecutors dropped a separate case against him in 2012 for a 67,000 euro fine. He died in September 2015.

name: Jean-Pierre Valentini
summary: Trafigura's head for West Africa. Jailed in Abidjan with Claude Dauphin in September 2006, on accusations of breaking toxic waste law and poisoning. Freed in February 2007 after the settlement. No trial of him appears on the pages opened.

name: Salomon Ugborugbo
summary: Owner of Compagnie Tommy, the Abidjan company whose trucks dumped the Probo Koala waste at 17 sites. Convicted of poisoning and sentenced to 20 years in October 2008.

name: Ira Rennert
summary: Billionaire owner of the Renco Group, whose companies bought the La Oroya smelter in Peru from the government in 1997. A US court called him the controlling owner of all the corporate defendants in the suit over children's lead poisoning. A $150 million settlement of more than a thousand claims was announced in June 2026, just before trial. Almost 3,000 claims remain.

name: Bill Turner
summary: Perth-based chief executive of Anvil Mining when an army operation at Kilwa, DR Congo, in October 2004 killed at least 73 civilians. UN investigators found Anvil planes and vehicles carried troops. Asked about it on Australian TV he said "So what! So what!"

name: Alberto Rotondo
summary: Tahoe Resources' security chief at the Escobal mine when guards fired on protesters on 27 April 2013. Charged in Guatemala with causing injury and obstructing justice; a judge sent him to trial in December 2014. He fled house arrest in November 2015. By 2017 he was in police custody in Peru awaiting extradition. No verdict appears on any page opened.

name: Mynor Padilla
summary: Head of security at Hudbay's Fenix mine in Guatemala. Acquitted in 2017 over the 2009 killing of Adolfo Ich and the shooting of German Chub; an appeal court ordered a new trial. He then pleaded guilty to homicide in an emotional state and to culpable injury, and a Guatemalan judge accepted the pleas in January 2021, with sentences already served and compensation.

name: Jaime Fernández-Cuesta Luca de Tena
summary: President of Repsol Peru at the 15 January 2022 La Pampilla spill, about 11,900 barrels per Al Jazeera. Prosecutors investigated him for environmental pollution, and a judge barred him and three others from leaving Peru for 18 months in January 2022. No charge in court, verdict or dismissal appears on any page opened.

name: Ly Yong Phat
summary: Cambodian senator and part-owner of the two companies given the Koh Kong sugar concessions in 2006, with Thailand's Khon Kaen Sugar and Taiwan's Ve Wong. 450 families were evicted in 2006, according to the NGOs' complaint. RFA cites a 2017 Politico report alleging he sent military police to burn villagers' crops. He has not been charged over the concessions on any page opened.

posts.org: Koh Kong Sugar Industry and Koh Kong Plantation

name: Charles Dennis Keiser
summary: General manager, Banadex (Chiquita in Colombia), 1989-2000. One of seven former Chiquita executives convicted in Colombia in July 2025 of aggravated conspiracy for financing the AUC paramilitaries, sentenced to 11 years and 3 months. The ruling was not final: arrest orders follow only once it is, and the defence said it would appeal. No appeal ruling appears on any page opened.

name: Álvaro Acevedo González
summary: General manager, Banadex (Chiquita in Colombia), from 2001. One of seven former Chiquita executives convicted in Colombia in July 2025 of aggravated conspiracy for financing the AUC paramilitaries, sentenced to 11 years and 3 months. The ruling was not final: arrest orders follow only once it is, and the defence said it would appeal. No appeal ruling appears on any page opened.

name: Víctor Julio Buitrago Sandoval
summary: Director of security, Banadex (Chiquita in Colombia), 1999-2004. One of seven former Chiquita executives convicted in Colombia in July 2025 of aggravated conspiracy for financing the AUC paramilitaries, sentenced to 11 years and 3 months. The ruling was not final: arrest orders follow only once it is, and the defence said it would appeal. No appeal ruling appears on any page opened.

name: Roderick Hills
summary: Chiquita board member who headed its audit committee, and a former US SEC chairman. In April 2003 he told Justice Department official Michael Chertoff that Chiquita was paying a paramilitary group on the US terrorist list. Payments went on for nearly another year. Prosecutors decided in 2007 not to charge him. He died in October 2014.

posts.role: Board member, head of audit committee

name: José Miguel Linares Martínez
summary: President of Drummond Ltd. in Colombia since 2013, earlier its vice-president of legal. Colombian prosecutors accuse him of helping finance the AUC paramilitaries in Cesar from 1996 to 2001 through an inflated food supply contract. In May 2023 the accusation was upheld and the case sent to trial. No verdict appears on any page opened.

name: Augusto Jiménez Mejía
summary: Former president of Drummond Ltd. in Colombia. Colombian prosecutors accuse him of helping finance the AUC paramilitaries in Cesar from 1996 to 2001 through an inflated food supply contract. In May 2023 the accusation was upheld and the case sent to trial. No verdict appears on any page opened.

posts.years: 1989-2019 per El Espectador; 1990-2012 per Climate Home

name: Brian Anderson
summary: Managing director of Shell's Nigerian company in 1995 and a named defendant in the US suit over the killing of Ken Saro-Wiwa (Wiwa v. Anderson). The suits were settled in June 2009 for $15.5 million with no admission of guilt, so the claims were never tried. Shell called the payment a humanitarian gesture.

posts.org: Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria

name: John Imle
summary: President of Unocal during the Yadana pipeline in Burma, where the army used forced labour. In 1995 he told a Greenpeace campaigner: "if you threaten the pipeline there's gonna be more military." He was a named defendant; Unocal settled in 2005 on confidential terms.

name: Miguel Facussé
summary: Owner of Corporación Dinant, the palm oil firm lent money by the World Bank's IFC. The IFC's complaint office audit said Dinant was linked by specific allegations to at least 40 of 100 targeted killings in the Bajo Aguán from 2010 to May 2013, according to 100Reporters. He was not convicted of any crime on the pages opened. He died in June 2015, aged 91.

name: Lenir Pérez
summary: Owner of Inversiones Los Pinares, the iron ore mine at Guapinol. Honduran prosecutors charged him and twelve others in 2024 with illegal exploitation of natural resources and aggravated environmental damage. He returned from the US, pleaded not guilty in March 2026 and was released on a $300,000 bond. His initial hearing was suspended on 17 September 2026 and set to resume 1 October; no result appears on any page opened. He is not charged over the killing of river defender Juan López.

name: Aden Duale
summary: Kenya's Defence Cabinet Secretary in June 2024. He announced the army's deployment on 25 June 2024 'in support of the National Police Service' during the Finance Bill protests (Citizen Digital). No page opened ties the deployment to a specific death.

name: Kamau Thugge
summary: Principal Secretary at Kenya's Treasury in 2018. Business Daily (2 March 2018) reports him saying petroleum products would attract 16% VAT from September, and says this was in line with a deal Kenya made with the IMF two years earlier.

name: Bola Tinubu
summary: President of Nigeria. In a broadcast on 4 August 2024, during the #EndBadGovernance protests, he said he had taken the 'painful yet necessary decision to remove fuel subsidies and abolish multiple foreign exchange systems'. Amnesty International later said at least 24 protesters were killed; police reject that report. No page opened shows an order from him on the police response.

name: Kayode Egbetokun
summary: Nigeria's Inspector-General of Police during the August 2024 protests. On the eve of the protests he told officers nationwide to 'deal decisively with any act of arson, intimidation or harassment' (Channels TV). Amnesty International said at least 24 protesters were killed and 1,200 arrested; his force rejects that. He resigned on 24 February 2026, citing family reasons. No court finding against him appears on the pages opened.

name: Goodluck Jonathan
summary: President of Nigeria. He removed the fuel subsidy on 1 January 2012 and defended it, calling the subsidies 'economically unsustainable' (RNZ). Petrol prices more than doubled. Al Jazeera reported three people killed on 9 January, one of them by police gunfire in Lagos per witnesses and hospital sources. On 16 January he announced a cut in the price (Christian Science Monitor).

name: Daniel Noboa
summary: President of Ecuador. His Decree 126 of 12 September 2025 ended the diesel subsidy and raised prices by over 50%, per Human Rights Watch. His decree of 16 September declared a state of emergency in 7 provinces and led to the armed forces being deployed. The Alliance for Human Rights in Ecuador reported two deaths and at least 296 injured as of 18 October.

name: Guillermo Lasso
summary: President of Ecuador during the June 2022 national strike. He issued a state of emergency decree on 17 June (No. 455) and replaced it on 20 June with one covering six provinces and banning assembly in public spaces, per El Comercio. He then announced a 10-cent-a-gallon cut in petrol, reported on 27 June. Al Jazeera reported at least six killed in clashes with security forces.

name: María Paula Romo
summary: Ecuador's Minister of Government during the October 2019 strike. On 25 November 2020 the National Assembly censured and removed her, 104 of 134 present voting yes. The grounds were use of expired tear gas and police repression at centres housing Indigenous protesters. This is a political censure, not a court finding.

name: Rafael Correa
summary: President of Ecuador. By executive decree he extended the state of exception in Morona Santiago on 12 January 2017, suspending rights including assembly and free movement (Vistazo). He said it was 'a lie' that the Nankints area was ancestral land. Police had evicted the 32 people of Nankints on 11 August 2016; no page says who ordered that.

name: Javier Milei
summary: President of Argentina. He vetoed an 8.1% pension rise in September 2024 and, in August 2025, a 7.2% pension rise and related pension and disability bills. Police used pepper spray and rubber bullets outside Congress on 11 September 2024 after the lower house failed to override the first veto. Congress overrode the disability veto in 2025.

name: Patricia Bullrich
summary: Argentina's Security Minister at the 12 March 2025 pensioners' protest. MercoPress reports she enforced an anti-picketing protocol; 124 people were arrested. A tear gas canister fired by a gendarme struck photographer Pablo Grillo in the head. On 17 March she took responsibility for the police response. A judge ordered the gendarme prosecuted in October 2025; Bullrich is not reported as charged.

name: Mauricio Macri
summary: President of Argentina. On 8 May 2018 he announced talks with the IMF for a financing line, and on 29 August 2018 announced an agreement with the IMF to advance funds. VOA says he committed to balancing the budget at the IMF's request; police fired rubber bullets at protesters outside Congress during the budget debate on 24 October 2018. No page opened shows an order from him to police.

name: Nicolás Dujovne
summary: Argentina's Treasury Minister in 2018. At the news conference on the June 2018 IMF deal he said the 2019 fiscal deficit target would fall to 1.3% of GDP from 2.2%, and that about 30% of the money would arrive after board approval.

name: Ranil Wickremesinghe
summary: President of Sri Lanka in 2023. On about 28 February 2023 he used executive powers to require 'essential services' staff to stay at work, in effect banning strikes against tax rises (Al Jazeera). Al Jazeera also reports he told union leaders he could not lower income taxes because the IMF required it.

name: Kanchana Wijesekera
summary: Sri Lanka's Power and Energy Minister. He announced a 66% rise in electricity prices on 16 February 2023, saying the country 'had no choice but to move toward cost-reflective pricing'.

name: Peter Breuer
summary: IMF official who, with Masahiro Nozaki, led the staff mission to Colombo from 24 August to 1 September 2022. The two issued the joint statement announcing the US$2.9 billion staff-level agreement, which listed cost-recovery pricing for fuel and electricity and major tax reforms. No page opened shows him setting a specific term.

posts.role: Co-lead of the staff mission to Sri Lanka

name: Ajith Nivard Cabraal
summary: Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka from September 2021 to 4 April 2022. In January 2022 he defended paying a US$500 million bond, saying postponing it 'would only aggravate problems' (AP). In November 2023 the Supreme Court found respondents including him responsible for the economic crisis and in breach of Article 12(1). Not a criminal conviction.

name: Gotabaya Rajapaksa
summary: President of Sri Lanka in the 2019-2022 period the Supreme Court reviewed. In November 2023 the court ruled 4-1 that a group including him breached the public trust and Article 12(1) through economic mismanagement. It was a fundamental rights ruling with about $458 in costs and no compensation. The reports opened do not show a personal decision of his on the bond payment.

posts.years: in post within the 2019-2022 period the court reviewed, including April 2022

name: Basil Rajapaksa
summary: Sri Lankan Finance Minister until President Gotabaya Rajapaksa removed him on 4 April 2022. In November 2023 the Supreme Court ruled 4-1 that a group including him breached the public trust and Article 12(1) through economic mismanagement. It was a fundamental rights ruling with about $458 in costs and no compensation. The reports opened do not show a personal decision of his on the bond payment.

name: Mostafa Madbouly
summary: Prime Minister of Egypt. On 29 May 2024 he announced a 300% rise in the price of subsidized bread, from 5 to 20 piasters a loaf, from June. About two-thirds of Egyptians use the subsidy programme.

name: Tarek Amer
summary: Governor of the Central Bank of Egypt in 2016. He announced the float of the pound at a press conference on 3 November 2016 and said 'A bold decision was vital to reform the monetary and exchange rate policies'. He had backed the IMF deal agreed on 11 August 2016.

name: Chris Jarvis
summary: IMF head of delegation for Egypt in 2016. He led the mission to Cairo from 30 July that reached the US$12 billion staff-level deal on 11 August and spoke at the press conference. He said the VAT 'is in parliament' and 'the government's fuel subsidy reform program continues to unfold'. No page opened shows him setting a specific term.

name: Miftah Ismail
summary: Pakistan's Finance Minister in 2022. He announced a 30-rupee-a-litre rise in petrol and diesel on 26 May 2022, a day after IMF talks failed over fuel and power subsidies. He said the Fund 'refused to grant further loan until we raise prices'.

name: Ken Ofori-Atta
summary: Ghana's Finance Minister in 2022. Presenting the 2023 budget in November 2022 he said VAT would rise from 12.5% to 15%. On 13 December 2022, at the press conference on the IMF deal, he committed to raising revenue by 1.2 points of GDP and cutting spending by about 2 points in 2023.

name: Hani Mulki
summary: Prime Minister of Jordan until 4 June 2018. On 2 June 2018 he refused union demands to withdraw the IMF-backed tax bill, which proposed raising income tax by at least 5%, saying lawmakers would decide (Arab News). He resigned on 4 June after mass protests.

name: Bisher Khasawneh
summary: Prime Minister of Jordan in 2022. On 5 December 2022 he told parliament the government would stop fuel subsidies because 'the Treasury does not have the luxury of subsidising fuel prices again'.

name: Hassan Abdallat
summary: Jordan's Attorney General in 2020. Human Rights Watch says he ordered the two-year closure of the Jordan Teachers Syndicate. On 25 July 2020 police raided its offices and arrested all 13 board members. The government had frozen public sector pay rises in April 2020.

name: Omar al-Bashir
summary: President of Sudan until April 2019. He announced the end of fuel subsidies in a speech on 22 September 2013. Human Rights Watch reports credible evidence of 170 deaths in the protests that followed. Over the protests from December 2018, prosecutors charged him in May 2019 with inciting and participating in the killing of demonstrators. No verdict on that charge appears on the pages opened.

name: Gibril Ibrahim
summary: Sudan's Finance Minister in 2021 (Arab News spells him Jibril Ibrahim). His ministry ended fuel subsidies on 8 June 2021: petrol went from 150 to 290 pounds a litre and diesel from 125 to 285. He called the old policy 'a failed and unfair policy where citizens are not equal'.

name: Volodymyr Zelensky
summary: President of Ukraine. He told parliament on 30 March 2020 'the two main conditions were the land law and the banking law' for an IMF loan. On 28 April 2020 he signed the land law, No. 552-IX.

name: Volodymyr Groysman
summary: Prime Minister of Ukraine. In April 2016 his government nearly doubled household gas tariffs, from about 3,600 to 6,879 hryvnias per 1,000 cubic metres. He called it 'difficult but essential for our country'. Business Recorder ties the rise to frozen IMF and Western aid.

name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
summary: President of Zimbabwe. He announced a fuel price rise in January 2019, taking petrol from $1.34 to $3.31 a litre. Human Rights Watch says security forces killed 17 people between 14 January and 5 February. On 22 January he called violence by security forces 'unacceptable', said 'If required, heads will roll', and called the fuel rise 'the right thing to do'.

name: Kurmanbek Bakiyev
summary: President of Kyrgyzstan until April 2010. On 25 July 2014 the Supreme Court sentenced him in absentia to life in prison for orchestrating the response to the April 2010 protests, in which AP reports 77 died. He lives in Belarus, which has refused to extradite him.

name: Zhanybek Bakiyev
summary: Brother of Kurmanbek Bakiyev and former head of Kyrgyzstan's State Security Service; also spelled Janysh. He too received a life sentence in absentia on 25 July 2014 over the response to the April 2010 protests. AP reported he lives in Belarus.

name: Manuel Chang
summary: Mozambique's Finance Minister when he signed state guarantees on over US$2 billion in loans; the loans broke the 2013 and 2014 budget ceilings, per AIM. A New York court convicted him in August 2024 of wire fraud and money laundering. He got 8.5 years in January 2025. He left US prison on 26 March 2026 and was deported; Legalbrief reports he landed in Mozambique on 5 April.

posts.years: in post when he signed the guarantees for the 2013-2014 loans

name: Gregório Leão
summary: Former director-general of Mozambique's intelligence service. A Maputo court convicted him on 7 December 2022 of embezzlement and abuse of power in the US$2 billion hidden debt scandal and sentenced him to 12 years. He was contesting the conviction at the Supreme Court as of December 2024. He was released on parole on 19 June 2025 (Lusa).

posts.org: Mozambique State Intelligence and Security Service (SISE)
posts.years: in post during the loans; dates not on the pages opened

name: Riah Phiyega
summary: South Africa's National Police Commissioner at Marikana on 16 August 2012, where police shot dead 34 striking miners. The Farlam Commission found the report to the president 'was deliberately amended' to hide a second shooting. The Claassen Board of Inquiry found her not fit for office (Daily Maverick). She was suspended in October 2015; her term ended 31 May 2017. Seri said in August 2026 that no one had been prosecuted over the events of 16 August.

name: Zukiswa Mbombo
summary: North West provincial police commissioner at Marikana in 2012. The Farlam Commission found she took the decision to remove strikers from the koppie by force if they did not lay down arms, and recommended an inquiry into her fitness for office. It found a prima facie case that she knew the true facts of the shootings. These are commission findings, not a conviction.

name: N. Venkatesh
summary: District Collector of Thoothukudi at the 22 May 2018 police firing, which killed 13 people protesting the Sterlite smelter. The Aruna Jagadeesan Commission criticised him for failing to hold talks with protesters and recommended departmental action. Tamil Nadu framed charges against him. He denied any lapses. South First reported in 2025 that no official had been punished.

name: Shailesh Kumar Yadav
summary: Inspector General of Police (South) at the 22 May 2018 Thoothukudi firing. The Aruna Jagadeesan Commission, tabled on 18 October 2022, found the firing unprovoked and said he should be held accountable, recommending departmental action. No criminal case against him appears on the pages opened; the CBI's chargesheets name one police officer, an inspector.

posts.role: Inspector General of Police (South), Tamil Nadu

name: P. Mahendran
summary: Superintendent of Police in Thoothukudi at the 22 May 2018 Thoothukudi firing. The Aruna Jagadeesan Commission, tabled on 18 October 2022, found the firing unprovoked and said he should be held accountable, recommending departmental action. No criminal case against him appears on the pages opened; the CBI's chargesheets name one police officer, an inspector.

name: Aleksandar Vučić
summary: Prime Minister of Serbia in 2014. He announced cuts to public pay of about 10% and to pensions of 3.1% to 10% in a television interview on 18 September 2014 (Novinite). WSWS reports the IMF called cuts of about €400 million the 'key condition' for a new loan.

name: Goran Vesić
summary: Serbia's Construction, Traffic and Infrastructure Minister when the Novi Sad station canopy fell in November 2024, killing 16. Prosecutors indicted him and 12 others on 16 September 2025 for serious offences against public safety. A lower court ended proceedings against him and five others; on 13 July 2026 N1 reported the Court of Appeals overturned that, so the trial can go ahead. He is charged, not convicted, and denies responsibility.

posts.role: Minister of Construction, Traffic and Infrastructure

name: Mia Mottley
summary: Prime Minister of Barbados. In October 2018, after Barbados entered a US$290 million IMF facility, she flagged public sector layoffs and said they were unlikely to exceed 1,500 people over the next few weeks. 'But, regrettably, one is too many,' she said.

name: Kun Kim
summary: A senior Cambodian general. The US Treasury says the Chinese company Union Development Group used Cambodian military forces 'provided through Kim' to intimidate villagers at the Dara Sakor project. Treasury sanctioned him on 9 December 2019 for corruption. This is a sanctions finding, not a court verdict.

name: Ollanta Humala
summary: President of Peru in 2015. On 29 September 2015 he issued a decree for a 30-day state of emergency in six provinces of Cusco and Apurímac after protests at the Las Bambas mine (VOA). About 1,500 police and 150 soldiers were sent. Three people died per VOA and Peru Reports; the Observatory of Mining Conflicts reported four.

name: George Papandreou
summary: Prime Minister of Greece in 2010. He announced the cuts and tax rises behind the first bailout at a televised cabinet meeting, €30 billion over three years, including cuts to public pay and pensions. Parliament passed the bill on 6 May 2010 with 172 votes. Three bodies were found in the wreckage of a Marfin Bank branch during that week's riots (fire brigade via WBUR); the map case says unidentified attackers threw the petrol bombs, and no page ties him to that attack.

name: George Papaconstantinou
summary: Greece's Finance Minister in 2010. On 2 May 2010 he announced a three-year public sector pay freeze, pension reductions, higher sales and fuel taxes and a higher effective retirement age under the €110 billion bailout.

name: Alexis Tsipras
summary: Prime Minister of Greece in 2015. He took the third bailout of €86 billion through parliament on 14 August 2015, saying 'I do not regret my decision to compromise'. On 17 October his majority passed a further bill raising the retirement age to 67 over seven years, which he called 'painful, but necessary'.

name: Poul Thomsen
summary: IMF official who headed the Fund's Greek programme and presented it to the IMF board on 9 May 2010. In a January 2013 interview he said 'Cuts in pensions and wages were necessary'. The Reuters report on the 2010 programme does not credit him with negotiating wages or pensions.

name: Nicos Anastasiades
summary: President of Cyprus in 2013. He negotiated for 12 hours in Brussels and accepted the 25 March 2013 deal that wound up Laiki bank and used deposits above €100,000 to recapitalise Bank of Cyprus, for €10 billion in loans. He said he was 'content' with it.

name: Jeroen Dijsselbloem
summary: President of the Eurogroup in 2013. He announced the Cyprus deal of 25 March 2013: Laiki bank wound up, deposits under €100,000 protected and those above facing losses. He said: 'We've put an end to the uncertainty'.

name: Traian Băsescu
summary: President of Romania in 2010. He announced, reported on 7 May 2010, that public pay would be cut by 25% and pensions by 15%. Romania's Constitutional Court later ruled some of the proposed cuts unconstitutional; media and unions said that concerned the pension cuts.

name: Germano Silva Lopes
summary: Former Samarco manager of structural projects (projetos estruturantes). Convicted on 3 September 2026 by Brazil's TRF-6 federal appeal court, in a unanimous ruling, of causing a flood resulting in death and of environmental crimes over the 2015 Fundão dam collapse, which killed 19 people. Sentence: 8 years 9 months in prison, starting in the closed regime, plus 192 day-fines. Appeals are still open. The pages opened do not set out what this manager personally did.

posts.role: Manager of structural projects (Projetos Estruturantes); Diário do Grande ABC calls the post general manager (gerente-geral)

name: Daviély Rodrigues Silva
summary: Former Samarco manager of geotechnics (geotecnia). Convicted on 3 September 2026 by Brazil's TRF-6 federal appeal court, in a unanimous ruling, of causing a flood resulting in death and of environmental crimes over the 2015 Fundão dam collapse, which killed 19 people. Sentence: 8 years 9 months in prison, starting in the closed regime, plus 192 day-fines. Appeals are still open. The pages opened do not set out what this manager personally did.

name: Wagner Milagres Alves
summary: Former Samarco manager of mine operations (operações de mina). Convicted on 3 September 2026 by Brazil's TRF-6 federal appeal court, in a unanimous ruling, of causing a flood resulting in death and of environmental crimes over the 2015 Fundão dam collapse, which killed 19 people. Sentence: 7 years 3 months 14 days in prison by the prosecutors' count (some reports say 15 days), starting in the semi-open regime, plus 160 day-fines. Appeals are still open. The pages opened do not set out what this manager personally did.

posts.role: Manager of mine operations (Operações de Mina); Diário do Grande ABC calls the post general manager (gerente-geral)

name: Chen Yuan-cheng
summary: Chairman of Formosa Ha Tinh Steel on 30 June 2016, in most reports; some say president. His name is also spelled Chen Yuan Cheng (陳源成), and Vietnamese papers write it Trần Nguyên Thành. A film clip of him apologising for the plant's discharge and the mass fish deaths was shown at the Vietnamese government's news conference that day. He is described only as speaking: no page opened shows him charged, or shows an act of his own in the discharge.

posts.role: Invited as vice chairman and chief executive (Taipei Times); named president (Kallanish)
posts.years: joined Formosa 1 August 2014 (Kallanish); Kallanish's report naming him president is dated 6 January, with no year shown on the page opened

posts.role: Chairman (most reports); President (Vietnam Government Portal, VTV, VOA photo caption)
posts.years: on 30 June 2016; start date not found

name: Kapil Kumar C Saratkar
summary: Deputy inspector general of police, Tirunelveli Range, at the Thoothukudi police firing of 22-23 May 2018, in which 13 people were killed (Scroll; UNI). The Aruna Jagadeesan Commission named him among 17 police personnel for departmental action, "without prejudice to launching criminal action". A commission is not a court. It found that one shooting took place at his instance and a deputy superintendent's, and another by a gunman on his instructions, both without the inspector general's knowledge. The pages opened do not say whether anyone was killed in those two shootings. He has not been cha

posts.role: Inspector General and Commissioner of Police, Madurai City

name: Alberto Fujimori
summary: President of Peru, 1990-2000. Prosecutors accused him as an indirect perpetrator (autor mediato) of the 1990s sterilisation programme: grave injury followed by death of five women and grave injury to about 1,300. A judge opened proceedings in December 2021, with his part suspended pending Chile's view on his extradition; the courts later annulled them. He was never tried on this and died in September 2024. Prosecutors archived the file in October 2026 as time-barred; the victims' lawyers say they will seek review.

name: Marino Costa Bauer
summary: Peru's health minister, April 1996 to January 1999, the years of the campaigns. Prosecutors say a document he signed set the ministry's plan for 150,000 tubal ligations in 1997 (CNN Chile). They accused him as an indirect perpetrator; a senior prosecutor had ordered him tried as co-author of grave injury. A judge opened proceedings in December 2021, which were later annulled. Never tried or convicted. The file was archived in October 2026 as time-barred; the victims' lawyers say they will seek review.

name: Eduardo Yong Motta
summary: Peru's health minister, October 1994 to April 1996. Gestión, setting out the prosecution's case, names him as drafter of the Programa de Salud Reproductiva y Planificación Familiar 1996-2000, the plan prosecutors say was used to legalise the sterilisations. They accused him as an indirect perpetrator; a senior prosecutor had ordered him tried as co-author of grave injury. A judge opened proceedings in December 2021, which were later annulled. Never tried or convicted. The file was archived in October 2026 as time-barred; the victims' lawyers say they will seek review.

name: Tika Ram Adhikari
summary: Chief warden of Chitwan National Park in 2006, when Shikharam Chaudhary died after detention by park staff. He told investigators he approved a 15-day investigation; he told the Kathmandu Post he saw the man only once. Suspended by the ministry and charged with homicide with two others; the district court ordered them held on remand. Nepal's Cabinet dismissed the case on 4 March 2007, so there was no verdict. He later became director general of the national parks department. He says the death was caused by illness.

posts.org: Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, Nepal

name: Kamal Jung Kunwar
summary: Assistant warden and head of the anti-poaching unit at Chitwan National Park in 2006. Charged with homicide over the death of Shikharam Chaudhary, whose wife says the dead man named him as a torturer. Nepal's Cabinet dismissed the case on 4 March 2007, so there was no verdict. WWF later gave him an award. He says it was interrogation, not torture.

posts.role: Assistant warden; head of Anti-Poaching Operations Unit

posts.years: at the time of the Post report (2019)

name: Abd al-Rahman Milad (Bija)
summary: Commander of the Libyan coast guard unit at Zawiya. The UN Security Council sanctioned him in 2018, citing its Panel of Experts that he was directly involved in sinking migrant boats with firearms. Arrested in Tripoli in about October 2020; Tripoli's military attorney general dropped the charges for lack of evidence in April 2021. Never convicted on the pages opened. Killed on 1 September 2024.

posts.role: Commander, Zawiya unit (suspended and dismissed after the sanctions, per The New Arab)

posts.org: Libyan coast guard and naval academy

name: Osama Elmasry Njeem
summary: Alleged to have run prison facilities in Tripoli including Mitiga. The ICC issued a warrant on 18 January 2025 for war crimes and crimes against humanity from February 2015, including murder, torture and rape of detainees; the warrant stands and he has not been tried there. New Lines says he led judicial police that intercepted migrants at sea. Arrested in Turin and flown back to Libya within days. Convicted in Tripoli: the attorney general's office announced on 21 June 2026 a sentence of 7 years 4 months for violating detainees' rights. That is a lesser and narrower case than the ICC's. Wheth

posts.role: Alleged by the ICC to be in charge of prison facilities

name: Paolo Gentiloni
summary: As Italy's prime minister he signed the Italy-Libya migration memorandum in Rome on 2 February 2017. The memorandum committed Italy to "technical and technological support to Libyan bodies in charge of the fight against illegal immigration", which Il Sole 24 Ore says include the border and coast guard under Libya's defence ministry, and to funding what it calls temporary reception centres under the "exclusive control" of Libya's interior ministry (EU Migration Law Blog). A UN investigator said in 2023 that EU and member state support has aided and abetted crimes in Libya, while saying they did

name: Fayez al-Serraj
summary: Head of Libya's UN-backed Government of National Accord. He signed the migration memorandum with Italy in Rome on 2 February 2017. The memorandum committed Italy to "technical and technological support to Libyan bodies in charge of the fight against illegal immigration", which Il Sole 24 Ore says include the border and coast guard under Libya's defence ministry, and to funding what it calls temporary reception centres under the "exclusive control" of Libya's interior ministry (EU Migration Law Blog). Those are bodies of the government he headed. No court or prosecutor has made a finding agains

name: John C. Cutler
summary: US Public Health Service doctor who led the 1946-1948 experiments in Guatemala, deliberately exposing about 1,300 prisoners, soldiers, psychiatric patients and sex workers to syphilis, gonorrhoea or chancroid, with NIH grant money. A US presidential commission said in 2011 of him and the other researchers: 'Their failure to exercise moral leadership cannot be excused.' A commission is not a court; no charge on any page opened. He died in 2003.

name: Théoneste Bagosora
summary: Director of cabinet at Rwanda's defence ministry in 1994, convicted by the UN Rwanda tribunal of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In the BNP case, complainants and Open Secrets say he went to the Seychelles in June 1994 to buy arms from Willem Ehlers, and that $1.3 million moved from the Rwandan central bank's BNP account to Ehlers. That payment is alleged, and no court has ruled on it. He died in 2021.

name: Georges Chodron de Courcel
summary: Group chief operating officer of BNP Paribas. New York's banking regulator says that at a September 2005 meeting, called by Geneva compliance officers over transactions for Sudanese customers, he dismissed their concerns and asked that no minutes be taken. The regulator lists him among 13 people who left the bank as a result of its investigation. Not personally charged on any page opened. BNP pleaded guilty as a company. The bank said in 2014 that he stepped down at his own request.

posts.years: at September 2005; stood down 30 June 2014, retiring 30 September 2014 (BNP Paribas)

name: Herminio Disini
summary: Associate of Ferdinand Marcos who, the Supreme Court found, acted as Special Sales Representative for Westinghouse and Burns & Roe on the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant. The Court held on 15 January 2021 that he used his closeness to Marcos to steer the contract, and ordered damages. It reduced the award in a resolution dated 29 August 2023 and made public in February 2024, which falls on his estate. Civil, not criminal. He died in June 2014.

name: António Carlos do Rosário
summary: Head of economic intelligence at Mozambique's SISE security service and chair of Proindicus, Ematum and MAM, the three companies that took the hidden loans. Convicted by the Maputo City Court on 7 December 2022 of embezzlement and abuse of power: 12 years, and jointly ordered to pay $2.883 billion. He refused a presidential pardon in December 2024 because his appeal was pending at the Supreme Court. Freed on conditional release in June 2025.

years not given on pages opened

name: Surjan Singh
summary: Former senior Credit Suisse banker on the Mozambique loans. Pleaded guilty in the US over his part in a $2 billion fraud and money-laundering scheme; admitted receiving $5.7 million in unlawful payments (Swissinfo). Banned by the UK's financial regulator, reported March 2025. A US judge gave him no prison term in June 2025 for cooperating; he testified at two Brooklyn trials.

posts.role: Senior banker, reporting to Andrew Pearse
posts.years: title not given on pages opened

name: Michael Sheehan
summary: US owner and managing director of Debt Advisory International, and a director of Donegal International from January 1998. Donegal bought Zambia's debt to Romania for under $4 million and sued in London for about $55 million. Justice Andrew Smith, in the High Court judgment of February 2007, said of Sheehan and a colleague that "they were at times being deliberately evasive and even dishonest"; the Guardian quotes him calling Sheehan 'not merely careless but cavalier in presenting his evidence'. The settlement was held binding, and about $15.5 million was to be paid. Civil case; no charge on an

name: Jelena Tanasković
summary: Former acting director of Serbian Railways Infrastructure. Indicted over the Novi Sad station canopy collapse of 1 November 2024, which killed 16. Prosecutors say she opened the wing B lobby on 5 July 2024 knowing no technical inspection had been done and no occupancy permit issued. A court halted the case in December 2025; the Court of Appeal reinstated it in June 2026. Not tried; no conviction.

posts.years: at July 2024; start not given on pages opened

name: Nebojša Šurlan
summary: Former director of Serbian Railways Infrastructure. Indicted over the Novi Sad canopy collapse, which killed 16. Prosecutors say he ordered no regular inspections of the structure during his term and did not carry out special measures the railway directorate ordered in 2020 and a 2021 decision. The Higher Court confirmed the indictment against him in December 2025 and the Court of Appeal rejected his appeal in 2026. Pretrial detention was replaced by house arrest with monitoring in May 2025. Not tried; no conviction.

posts.years: before Jelena Tanasković; years not given on pages opened

name: Sapar Isakov
summary: Former Kyrgyz prime minister (August 2017 to April 2018), convicted on 6 December 2019 and given 15 years over the 2013 modernisation of the Bishkek power plant, which went to China's TBEA. On 29 April 2025 the Supreme Court annulled the conviction and ordered a new trial. Freed amid the October 2020 unrest, he is presumed to have left the country and is on a wanted list. No result of the retrial on any page opened.

posts.years: August 2017 to April 2018 (RFE/RL); his post during the 2013 project is not given on pages opened

name: Jantoro Satybaldiev
summary: Former Kyrgyz prime minister, whose government left office on 26 March 2014. Convicted on 6 December 2019 and given 7 and a half years over the 2013 modernisation of the Bishkek power plant, won by China's TBEA. The Supreme Court upheld the sentences in June 2020 and refused reviews in March and September 2021. He denies guilt. The plant's January 2018 accident left thousands of households without heat for days.

name: Aibek Kaliev
summary: Former head of Kyrgyzstan's National Energy Holding and former deputy energy minister. Convicted on 6 December 2019 and given 15 years over the 2013 modernisation of the Bishkek power plant by China's TBEA. Pardoned by President Japarov and freed, reported in September 2021. The Supreme Court refused his request to reopen the case on 21 October 2025.

posts.years: years not given on pages opened

name: Christian Herrault
summary: Lafarge deputy managing director. Convicted over the Syrian plant payments by the Paris court on 13 April 2026: five years in prison, immediate custody, €225,000 fine. Justice Info reports prosecutors treating him as one of two presumed decision-makers (présumés décideurs). The Paris Court of Appeal released him under judicial supervision in May 2026 ahead of an appeal trial. He says keeping the plant open protected staff.

posts.role: Deputy managing director (The National: deputy chief operating officer)
posts.years: years not given on pages opened

name: Bruno Pescheux
summary: Director of Lafarge Cement Syria, 2008 to July 2014. Convicted over the plant's payments by the Paris court on 13 April 2026: five years in prison, €225,000 fine. Justice Info says he was reportedly behind a 2013 email to Christian Herrault seeking to hide any link between the subsidiary and intermediary Firas Tlass. At trial he called himself an arranger, 'not a composer'.

name: Bernhard Esau
summary: Namibia's fisheries minister until he resigned in 2019. Charged in the Fishrot case, including fraud over quota allocation and tax evasion; he denied them at the plea stage. A High Court judge refusing him bail found a prima facie case: that he passed on a letter he knew held falsehoods, nominated an unregistered Angolan firm for quotas and approved the allocation. No verdict. He calls the charges 'outrageous and malicious'.

posts.org: Ministry of Fisheries and Marine Resources, Namibia

name: Sacky Shanghala
summary: Namibia's attorney general and justice minister until he resigned in 2019. Charged in the Fishrot case with fraud over quota allocation and tax evasion; a not-guilty plea was entered for him as he disputes the court's jurisdiction. A High Court judge said he signed a letter containing false information and recommended James Hatuikulipi to chair state firm Fishcor. Al Jazeera reports leaked documents showing close to $10 million from Samherji to businesses linked to him. No verdict.

posts.role: Attorney general and minister of justice

name: Charles Taylor
summary: Rebel leader in Liberia, later president. Met Firestone executives near Gbarnga in July 1991; his government signed a January 1992 memorandum with the company, and by the end of 1992 Firestone had paid out more than $2.3 million in taxes, pensions, worker injury funds and rent, about $1.3 million in cash or check and about $1 million in goods (court files, per Frontline). Convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone in April 2012 and given 50 years, upheld in September 2013, for crimes in Sierra Leone only. Never tried for harm in Liberia.

posts.org: NPFL and its self-declared government, Liberia

name: Gale Ruff
summary: Head of plantation operations and acting general manager of Firestone in Liberia. He signed the January 1992 memorandum with Charles Taylor's rebel government at Gbarnga, under which the company arranged payments to it. No charge against him on any page opened. He says he was handed a done deal.

posts.role: Head of operations for the farm; acting general manager

name: John Schremp
summary: Director of Firestone's Synthetic and Rubber Division in Akron, Ohio, which oversaw the Liberian plantation. Met Charles Taylor near Gbarnga on 3 July 1991; under his leadership Firestone entered the memorandum to pay Taylor's government taxes for protection, according to ProPublica. He wrote to Taylor: 'We found the discussions very enlightening and helpful.' No charge against him on any page opened.

posts.org: Firestone Synthetic and Rubber Division, Akron, Ohio

name: Carlos Sánchez Berzaín
summary: Bolivia's defence minister during the 2003 Gas War, in which forces killed 58 and injured over 400. In a US civil suit a jury found him liable for extrajudicial killings on 3 April 2018, with $10 million in damages. A judge overturned it, the appeals court vacated that ruling in 2020, and the parties settled on 28 September 2023 for an undisclosed sum. Civil, not criminal.

name: Võ Kim Cự
summary: Ha Tinh's top official when Formosa's steel plant was licensed. Vietnam's Party inspectors said he signed several Formosa documents and was mainly responsible for wrongdoings in 2008-2016; VnExpress says he approved licences and an illegal waste pipeline. The Party dismissed him from posts retroactively in April 2017, he lost his National Assembly seat in May 2017, and the prime minister stripped his titles. Inspectors said legal proceedings should start; no court case is on the pages opened.

posts.role: Vice chairman (2005-2010) and chairman (2010-2015) of the People's Committee; Party secretary; head of Economic Zone Management Board 2008-2010

name: Bùi Cách Tuyến
summary: Vietnam's deputy environment minister and head of its Environment Administration. Party inspectors found he 'acted irresponsibly in signing Formosa's environmental impact report' and weakened inspections of its environmental facilities. The Party dismissed him from a ministry Party post in April 2017, and a prime minister's decision stripped his title. Over Formosa, discipline only on the pages opened: no court case.

posts.org: Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, Vietnam
posts.role: Deputy minister; head of Environment Administration

name: Nguyễn Thái Lai
summary: Vietnam's deputy environment minister. Party inspectors found he 'acted irresponsibly in examining and signing Formosa's sewage discharge licence'. The Party dismissed him from a ministry Party post in April 2017, and a prime minister's decision stripped his title. Discipline only on the pages opened: no court case.

posts.org: Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, Vietnam
